messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 2019-10-31 at 09:56 -0700, James Grecian wrote:
> The model runs fine when there is no prediction data, but when I
> include the NAs I get the following error:
>
> file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: 0bed76828f01  date: Tue Sep 03 11:21:49
> 2019 +0300
> Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 876,
> Thread: 0
> Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...
>
> Can anyone shed light on why I might be getting this error?

Hi.

this is an error saying that the precision matrix is numerical singular.
Doing prediction, this could happen more easily, as long term prediction
can get highly non-informative. So doing one-step ahead prediction is easier than
doing predictions one year ahead.

The way out is to re-check your model if you have intrinsic model
components (like rw1/rw2, etc), that tends to get 'more singular' without data,
and maybe use proper model components instead. Also check the fit, that the model components
have a reasonable posterior variance.

Let me know
H

--
Håvard Rue
Helpdesk
he...@r-inla.org

normally, this is not in use, only if you define f(..., group=)

the issue is that its hard in the code to distinguish the case
this is not used and number of groups is 1 (or > 1). so, you can
just ignore it if you do not use it.

Best
H

Also, when using default gaussian model in INLA, is it always better to scale the response to standard Normal? I noticed when I scale the response, the posterior mean looks much closer to the data(I used default setting of gaussian model).

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] how to check if covariates are significant using INLA
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] how to check if covariates are significant using INLA
messages.body_plain:
AFAIK, the answer to your first question is no.

IMHO you should use sensible units for your response variable. Those units should match the magnitude of an expert's estimate of the response values. You express the distance between two cities in tens, hundreds or thousands of kilometers, not in meters. Let's assume that you use hundreds of km as a unit and measure the distance in meters. Then scale the response by a factor 1e5.
Doing this makes it much easier to interpret the model parameter as they in the same units as the response.

Best regards,

Hi,

For the first question: Different interpretations of this goal gives very very different procedures. From p values to model comparisons.

For the second question: Scale everything to a reasonable scale always. Both responses and covariates. Whoever implemented the numerical algorithms you use (e.g. INLA) assume that you have reasonable numerical values everywhere. Any default settings assume you have "standard looking data".

Haakon

Hi Håvard,

Many thanks for your reply.

The model fit seems to be ok. All the terms were linear and the prediction is essentially ‘one-step ahead’.

In this example the error arises when generating one spatial prediction from the data (so the prediction accounts for about 6% of the data frame). I was surprised to see the error when generating a relatively small number of spatial predictions.

Best,

James

>>

>
> Hi.
>
> this is an error saying that the precision matrix is numerical singular.
> Doing prediction, this could happen more easily, as long term prediction
> can get highly non-informative. So doing one-step ahead prediction is easier than
> doing predictions one year ahead.
>
> The way out is to re-check your model if you have intrinsic model
> components (like rw1/rw2, etc), that tends to get 'more singular' without data,
> and maybe use proper model components instead. Also check the fit, that the model components
> have a reasonable posterior variance.
>
>
> Let me know
> H
>
>
> --
> Håvard Rue
> Helpdesk
> he...@r-inla.org

messages.body_plain:
Looks like you’re using the wrong E value. I think you intended to use the “exposure” variable from the stack data (extract with inla.stack.data() before the inla call to make that more easily accessible). If this is a LGCP likelihood, I.e. with observations and exposure setup to construct a Cox point process likelihood, then it may be clearer to split into three sub stacks; one with y=1, one with y=0, and one with y=NA that only deals with the prediction.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Generating predictions from a space-time LGCP model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Generating predictions from a space-time LGCP model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

You’re right this is an LGCP likelihood. I have a column for observations (Y) and a column for exposure. However I have different numbers of individuals sampled in each period, so the exposure has been adjusted to account for this effect (exp_adj).

When Y is NA (i.e. for my prediction dataframe) I have used the unadjusted E that is estimated for the mesh.

Is that likely to cause the precision matrix to be numerical singular?

Many thanks,

James

> On 4 Nov 2019, at 13:50, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Looks like you’re using the wrong E value. I think you intended to use the “exposure” variable from the stack data (extract with inla.stack.data() before the inla call to make that more easily accessible). If this is a LGCP likelihood, I.e. with observations and exposure setup to construct a Cox point process likelihood, then it may be clearer to split into three sub stacks; one with y=1, one with y=0, and one with y=NA that only deals with the prediction.
>
> Finn
>
> > On 31 Oct 2019, at 16:56, James Grecian <jamesg...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > ﻿
> > Hi INLA users,
> >
> > I am fitting a space-time log Gaussian Cox process model with covariates and am coming unstuck when trying to generate spatial predictions. I would like to generate a lot of predictions from this model, somewhere in the region of 24 different spatial predictions of the entire mesh.
> >
> > Following the INLA tutorials I have tried to generate spatial predictions while fitting the model. I have appended a dataframe of covariate values from which I want to generate predictions and have included a column of NAs for the Y/ Frequency column. I have also specified link = 1 and compute = TRUE in the `control.predictor` argument.
> >
> > The model runs fine when there is no prediction data, but when I include the NAs I get the following error:
> >

> > Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 876, Thread: 0
> > Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...
> >
> > Can anyone shed light on why I might be getting this error?
> >
> > Following this post: http://www.r-inla.org/events/problemswithopenblas I have tried `inla.setOption(mkl = TRUE) but this does not resolve the issue.
> >
> > Alternatively, given that I am planning on generating so many predicted surfaces should I try an alternative method to generate predictions? For example by sampling from the posterior instead?
> >
> > Any help would be greatly appreciated!
> >
> > Many thanks,
> >
> > James
> >
> >

> >                          n.group = k,
> >                          mesh.group = tmesh)

> >                             n.spde = barrier.model$f$n,
> >                             n.group = k)

> >                                       x_bar_c_s_m = agg.dat$x_bar_c_s_m,
> >                                       x_res_smy = agg.dat$x_res_smy)))
> >
> > pcrho <- list(theta = list(prior = 'pccor1', param = c(.7, .7)))
> >
> > f_1 <- y ~ -1 + b0 + x_bar + x_bar_c_s + x_bar_c_s_m + x_res_smy +
> >   f(s,
> >     model = barrier.model,
> >     group = s.group,
> >     replicate = s.repl,

> >                          hyper = pcrho))

> >                                      link = 1,
> >                                      compute = TRUE),

messages.body_plain:
That sounds more like a regular geolocated Poisson _count_ model to me, but perhaps the integration weights and 0/1 values are hiding I setup code you didn’t quote?

Finn

> On 4 Nov 2019, at 16:41, James Grecian <jamesg...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿Hi Finn,

>
> You’re right this is an LGCP likelihood. I have a column for observations (Y) and a column for exposure. However I have different numbers of individuals sampled in each period, so the exposure has been adjusted to account for this effect (exp_adj).
>
> When Y is NA (i.e. for my prediction dataframe) I have used the unadjusted E that is estimated for the mesh.
>
> Is that likely to cause the precision matrix to be numerical singular?
>
> Many thanks,
>
> James
>
>
> > On 4 Nov 2019, at 13:50, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Looks like you’re using the wrong E value. I think you intended to use the “exposure” variable from the stack data (extract with inla.stack.data() before the inla call to make that more easily accessible). If this is a LGCP likelihood, I.e. with observations and exposure setup to construct a Cox point process likelihood, then it may be clearer to split into three sub stacks; one with y=1, one with y=0, and one with y=NA that only deals with the prediction.
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > > On 31 Oct 2019, at 16:56, James Grecian <jamesg...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > ﻿
> > > Hi INLA users,
> > >
> > > I am fitting a space-time log Gaussian Cox process model with covariates and am coming unstuck when trying to generate spatial predictions. I would like to generate a lot of predictions from this model, somewhere in the region of 24 different spatial predictions of the entire mesh.
> > >
> > > Following the INLA tutorials I have tried to generate spatial predictions while fitting the model. I have appended a dataframe of covariate values from which I want to generate predictions and have included a column of NAs for the Y/ Frequency column. I have also specified link = 1 and compute = TRUE in the `control.predictor` argument.
> > >
> > > The model runs fine when there is no prediction data, but when I include the NAs I get the following error:

> > > Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...

> > >
> > > Following this post: http://www.r-inla.org/events/problemswithopenblas I have tried `inla.setOption(mkl = TRUE) but this does not resolve the issue.
> > >
> > > Alternatively, given that I am planning on generating so many predicted surfaces should I try an alternative method to generate predictions? For example by sampling from the posterior instead?

> > > Any help would be greatly appreciated!
> > >
> > > Many thanks,

> > >                                       x_bar_c_s_m = agg.dat$x_bar_c_s_m,
> > >                                       x_res_smy = agg.dat$x_res_smy)))
> > >

> > >
> > > f_1 <- y ~ -1 + b0 + x_bar + x_bar_c_s + x_bar_c_s_m + x_res_smy +
> > >   f(s,
> > >     model = barrier.model,
> > >     group = s.group,

messages.subject: Fitting random effect interactions
messages.subject_clean: Fitting random effect interactions
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Very new to INLA - I'm trying to migrate a model I have working in MCMCglmm to INLA in order to account for an important spatial component in my data.

The model I have in MCMCglmm is specified like this:

model_simple_3 <- MCMCglmm(fixed = cbind(Abundance, Total.tips) ~ 1,
                  random = ~OTU + Family + Family:OTU,
                  family = "multinomial2",
                  data = OTU_matrix_long, nitt = 500000, prior = prior, thin = 40,
                  pr = F)

The idea is that any random effect specified without an interaction, if significant, provides a test for differences in alpha diversity between factor levels, while any random effect that interacts with OTU provides a test for beta diversity or community turnover between factor levels. There's a bunch of different factors I want to play with, but this is a simple example that I'd like to get working first.

I currently have this as my model specification in INLA:

formula2 <- y ~ -1 +
  f(spatial.field, model=spde) +
  f(OTU, model="iid") +
  f(Family, model="iid") +
  f(OTU2, model="iid",
    replicate = Family)

Mod2 <- inla(formula2,
            data = inla.stack.data(Stack, spde = spde),
            family = "binomial",
            control.compute = list(cpo = TRUE),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(Stack),
                                     compute=T),
            Ntrials = Data$Tot_Tips,
            verbose = F)

However, when I try running this model, I get the following error:

Error in Summary.factor(c(NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,  :
  ‘max’ not meaningful for factors

Is it possible to specify such a model in INLA, and if so, how does one do it?

Cheers,
Jim Downie

Hi Jim,

I assume one or several of OTU, Family, OTU2, and Family are stored as factors?
The NAs are introduced (by design) by inla.stack(), and different
models require different handling of factors with NAs.
In your case, it looks as if you could pre-transform the factors into
factor level indices instead, with as.numeric(), since they are all
just used for indexing into "iid" random effects.

> as.numeric(factor(c("b","c","a","b")))
[1] 2 3 1 2

This will give the same model as when using an actual factor variable
with an "iid" model, but relieves INLA from having to interpret the
factor variables by itself.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
In the LGCP likelihood setup, all rows with Freq=1 should have
exposure=0, and all exposure>0 rows should have Freq=0, some something
isn't right with the LGCP likelihood setup. (all rows shown have _both
Freq and exposure = 1.

Finn

On Wed, 6 Nov 2019 at 14:48, James Grecian <jamesg...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Finn,
>
> I’ve calculated integration weights based on the code in section 4 of the SPDE book. I didn’t include the whole code as it’s quite long. Here’s a clip from the data frame that is being fed to INLA. Y is Freq and E is adj_exp.

>
> On 4 Nov 2019, at 16:56, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> That sounds more like a regular geolocated Poisson _count_ model to me, but perhaps the integration weights and 0/1 values are hiding I setup code you didn’t quote?
>
> Finn
>
> On 4 Nov 2019, at 16:41, James Grecian <jamesg...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿Hi Finn,
>
> You’re right this is an LGCP likelihood. I have a column for observations (Y) and a column for exposure. However I have different numbers of individuals sampled in each period, so the exposure has been adjusted to account for this effect (exp_adj).
>
> When Y is NA (i.e. for my prediction dataframe) I have used the unadjusted E that is estimated for the mesh.
>
> Is that likely to cause the precision matrix to be numerical singular?
>
> Many thanks,
>
> James
>
>
> On 4 Nov 2019, at 13:50, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Looks like you’re using the wrong E value. I think you intended to use the “exposure” variable from the stack data (extract with inla.stack.data() before the inla call to make that more easily accessible). If this is a LGCP likelihood, I.e. with observations and exposure setup to construct a Cox point process likelihood, then it may be clearer to split into three sub stacks; one with y=1, one with y=0, and one with y=NA that only deals with the prediction.
>
> Finn
>
> On 31 Oct 2019, at 16:56, James Grecian <jamesg...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿
> Hi INLA users,
>
> I am fitting a space-time log Gaussian Cox process model with covariates and am coming unstuck when trying to generate spatial predictions. I would like to generate a lot of predictions from this model, somewhere in the region of 24 different spatial predictions of the entire mesh.
>
> Following the INLA tutorials I have tried to generate spatial predictions while fitting the model. I have appended a dataframe of covariate values from which I want to generate predictions and have included a column of NAs for the Y/ Frequency column. I have also specified link = 1 and compute = TRUE in the `control.predictor` argument.
>
> The model runs fine when there is no prediction data, but when I include the NAs I get the following error:
>
> file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: 0bed76828f01  date: Tue Sep 03 11:21:49 2019 +0300
> Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 876, Thread: 0
> Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...
>
> Can anyone shed light on why I might be getting this error?
>
> Following this post: http://www.r-inla.org/events/problemswithopenblas I have tried `inla.setOption(mkl = TRUE) but this does not resolve the issue.
>
> Alternatively, given that I am planning on generating so many predicted surfaces should I try an alternative method to generate predictions? For example by sampling from the posterior instead?
>
> Any help would be greatly appreciated!
>
> Many thanks,
>
> James
>
>
> Here is my model set up. I am working on a Windows server with 44 cores and 512GB memory.
>
> A.st <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = smesh,
>                          loc = smesh$loc[agg.dat$area, ],
>                          group = agg.dat$season,
>                          n.group = k,
>                          mesh.group = tmesh)
>
> idx <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 's',
>                             n.spde = barrier.model$f$n,
>                             n.group = k)
>
> stk <- inla.stack(data = list(y = agg.dat$Freq,
>                               exposure = agg.dat$exp_adj),
>                   A = list(A.st, 1),
>                   effects = list(idx,
>                                  list(b0 = rep(1, nrow(agg.dat)),
>                                       x_bar = agg.dat$x_bar,
>                                       x_bar_c_s = agg.dat$x_bar_c_s,
>                                       x_bar_c_s_m = agg.dat$x_bar_c_s_m,
>                                       x_res_smy = agg.dat$x_res_smy)))
>
> pcrho <- list(theta = list(prior = 'pccor1', param = c(.7, .7)))
>
> f_1 <- y ~ -1 + b0 + x_bar + x_bar_c_s + x_bar_c_s_m + x_res_smy +
>   f(s,
>     model = barrier.model,
>     group = s.group,
>     replicate = s.repl,
>     control.group = list(model = 'ar1',
>                          hyper = pcrho))
>
> m_1 <- inla(f_1,
>             family = 'poisson',
>             data = inla.stack.data(stk),
>             control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk),
>                                      link = 1,
>                                      compute = TRUE),
>             E = agg.dat$exp_adj,
>             control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian",
>                                 int.strategy = "eb"),
>             control.compute = list(openmp.strategy = "huge",
>                                    config = TRUE,
>                                    dic = T,
>                                    waic = T),
>                         control.mode = list(theta = c(1.323, 7.089, 0.643), restart = T),
>             verbose = T,
>             num.threads = 16) # switch on when trialling
>
> This is the verbose output from INLA when fitting the model and generating predictions:

Also notable is that the exposure column is completely different from
the exp_adj column, even though in the stack call you set exposure to
exp_adj.

Finn

> > Looks like you’re using the wrong E value. I think you intended to use the “exposure” variable from the stack data (extract with inla.stack.data() before the inla call to make that more easily accessible). If this is a LGCP likelihood, I.e. with observations and exposure setup to construct a Cox point process likelihood, then it may be clearer to split into three sub stacks; one with y=1, one with y=0, and one with y=NA that only deals with the prediction.

I have appended a dataframe of covariate values from which I want to generate predictions and have included a column of NAs for the Y/ Frequency column. messages.subject: Spatial downscaling on R-INLA
messages.subject_clean: Spatial downscaling on R-INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi R-INLA users,

I was wondering whether is possible to carry out spatial downscaling by using the R-INLA package.

For the sake of discussion, let's assume that the study area, D, is comprised of $m$ non overlapping regions, $R_i$, at which data is available. Let $y_i$ denotes the figure for region $R_i$. On the other hand, let's consider a finer misaligned partition of D comprised of $n$ non overlapping regions $S_j$, where $x_j$ denotes the underlying figure for $S_j$. Then, $y_i$ can be thought as a noisy realisation of the aggregate figures of $S_j$ regions which intersect $R_i$, y_i=A_i.x+e_i, where $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)^t$, $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)^t$, $A_{ij}$ is proportional to the area of $R_i \cap S_j$ and $e_i \sim N(0,\tau)$. In addition, let's assume that x_j=Z_j.\beta+u_i, where \beta are fixed effects and u_i is a spatially structured effect (u \sim GMRF).

The goal is to infer x. Is there a way to fit this framework by using R-INLA?

Best,
Roman.

messages.subject_clean: Separable space-time model + prediction via sampling: coding query
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm sure there's something I'm doing wrong but I can't figure it out. I'm fitting a separable space-time model in R-INLA, with the goal of doing prediction via sampling using inla.posterior.sample. The first issue has to do with the model fitting, which I am doing as follows:

knots=min(cattle_data@data$time):max(cattle_data@data$time)

mesh = inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain = loc.mesh,
                    max.edge = c(0.3,0.6),
                    offset = c(1, 1))

spde_RE<-inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha=2)

A<-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=coords_cattle, group=cattle_data@data$time, n.group=length(knots))

iset <- inla.spde.make.index('i', n.spde=spde_RE$n.spde, n.group=length(knots))

stk.dat.c<-inla.stack(
  data=list(resp=cattle_data@data$n.cattle),
  A=list(A,1),
  effects=list(c(iset, list(intercept=1)), list(cattle_data@data)),
  tag='est')

pcprior<-list(theta = list(prior = "pc.prec", params = c(3, 0.05)))

f.spde <- resp ~ 0 + intercept + urban + f(i, model=spde_RE, hyper = pcprior, group=i.group, control.group=list(model="ar1"))

res<-inla (f.spde, data=inla.stack.data(stk.dat.c), family="zeroinflatedpoisson1", offset=log(cattle_data@data$mem.cattle), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.dat.c)),
                      num.threads = inla.getOption("num.threads"), control.compute=list(config = TRUE), verbose=TRUE)

-------------------------
The dataset has 6,290 rows, the mesh has 1,428 vertices, and there are 17 knots in total. There is at least one row in the dataset (cattle_data) corresponding to each knot (i.e., each "time" value). My goal is to do prediction via sampling using inla.posterior.sample.

The A matrix is 6290 x 24276 as expected, but res$summary.random$i has 1,428 rows (that is, equal to the number of mesh vertices). I believe this should have # rows = # mesh vertices * # knots, that is 24,276. Is that correct? Similarly, the corresponding entry in res$misc$configs$contents$length is 1,428.

The second issue has to do with the mesh for prediction. My code for this is:
Aprd<-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc.pred, group=kIdx, n.group=length(knots))

Where "kIdx" is the group index (1-17), and there are 90,000 locations for prediction. This is a 1428 x 24276 matrix.

My thought is if the corresponding draw from inla.posterior.sample is of length 24276, I can then do draw%*%Aprd for prediction. Is my Aprd code a matrix to project from the space-time mesh, to a space only mesh at the indicated knot, and then I need a second matrix to project to the prediction locations?

Alternatively, if you can point me to an example of sampling via prediction on a separable space-time model, that would be helpful. As you may be able to tell, I am not a statistician!

Thanks,
Julianne

messages.subject_clean: Simulate Besag Spatial Effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi there, I am simulating spatial effects following the code of the besagproper.pdf of the inla.doc("besagproper") documentation.

In the notes in the last part of the documentation says that if d = 0 and the parameter rankdef=1 is set, then this model corresponds to the besag model.

The problem is that when I use d = 0 I get an error in the chol(Q) line. How could I simulate besag model effects?

library(INLA)
## pick a graph
graph = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")
g = inla.read.graph(graph)
## we will use replicated samples in our testing
nrep = 5
## make life easy; use dense matrix algebra
d = 0
tau = 1.0
Q = matrix(0, g$n, g$n)
diag(Q) = tau * (d + g$nnbs)
for(i in 1:g$n) {
  if (g$nnbs[i] > 0) {
    Q[i, g$nbs[[i]]] = -tau
    Q[g$nbs[[i]], i] = -tau
  }
 }
 R = chol(Q) ## 'chol' returns the upper triangular
 Error in chol.default(Q) :
  the leading minor of order 544 is not positive definite

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] crash without pardiso
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] crash without pardiso
messages.body_plain:
with taucs or pardiso with openmp.strategy='pardiso.serial', then the
parallisation is done by running serial factorisations on many
matrices in parallel, like

## do this loop in parallel
   for(i in 1:n)  Q.chol[[i]] = chol(Q[[i]])

this run efficient if the matrices are small enough, AND, there is
enough memory to handle all these

the other strategy, openmp.strategy='pardiso.parallel', is different,
it uses all cores to factorisize ONE, and only ONE, matrix at the
time, like

## do in parallel
	Q.chol = chol(Q)

this require much less memory, but is (in most cases) slower then the
serial strategy, IF, the serial strategy can work without any memory
issue.

since TAUCS is serial code only, and PARDISO is serial and parallel
code, then
the serial strategy works for TAUCS and PARDISO, while the parallel
one, only works for PARDISO.

for large models, as you have, yes, then chose
openmp.strategy='pardiso.parallel'

hope this helps,
H

messages.body_snippet:
Hi Finn,

Thanks for highlighting this. I hadn’t realised this was required in an LGCP model.

My particular analysis is for a space-time LGCP model and so I’ve been basing my code on section 8.4 of t

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Generating predictions from a space-time LGCP model
messages.body_plain:
Sec 8.4 aggregates the points into counts for a dual mesh, which turns the continuous Point process model into a discrete count model, via a zero-order integration approximation. The general LGCP likelihood approximation doesn’t do that.

Finn

>
> ﻿Hi Finn,
>
> Thanks for highlighting this. I hadn’t realised this was required in an LGCP model.
>
> My particular analysis is for a space-time LGCP model and so I’ve been basing my code on section 8.4 of the spde book. The data frame matches the structure of the data frame passed to INLA in section 8.4.
>
> Can you recommend another source of R code for structuring space-time LGCP models?
>
> Best,
>
> James
>
>

Hi Finn,

So is the model in 8.4 not a space-time LGCP?

Could this be why I’m running into singular matrix issues when generating predictions?

Best,

James

> On 11 Nov 2019, at 15:50, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Sec 8.4 aggregates the points into counts for a dual mesh, which turns the continuous Point process model into a discrete count model, via a zero-order integration approximation. The general LGCP likelihood approximation doesn’t do that.
>
> Finn
>
>> On 11 Nov 2019, at 15:36, James Grecian <jamesg...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> ﻿Hi Finn,
>>
>> Thanks for highlighting this. I hadn’t realised this was required in an LGCP model.
>>
>> My particular analysis is for a space-time LGCP model and so I’ve been basing my code on section 8.4 of the spde book. The data frame matches the structure of the data frame passed to INLA in section 8.4.
>>
>> Can you recommend another source of R code for structuring space-time LGCP models?
>>
>> Best,
>>
>> James
>>
>>
>>> On 6 Nov 2019, at 14:56, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> In the LGCP likelihood setup, all rows with Freq=1 should have
>>> exposure=0, and all exposure>0 rows should have Freq=0, some something
>>> isn't right with the LGCP likelihood setup. (all rows shown have _both
>>> Freq and exposure = 1.
>>>
>>> Finn
>>>

>>>> Looks like you’re using the wrong E value. I think you intended to use the “exposure” variable from the stack data (extract with inla.stack.data() before the inla call to make that more easily accessible). If this is a LGCP likelihood, I.e. with observations and exposure setup to construct a Cox point process likelihood, then it may be clearer to split into three sub stacks; one with y=1, one with y=0, and one with y=NA that only deals with the prediction.
>>>>
>>>> Finn

Hi Finn,

So is the model in 8.4 not a space-time LGCP?

Could this be why I’m running into singular matrix issues when generating predictions?

Best,

James

> On 11 Nov 2019, at 15:50, Finn Lindgren

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Generating predictions from a space-time LGCP model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Generating predictions from a space-time LGCP model
messages.body_plain:
It’s more a philosophical interpretation issue. It is a valid approximation of an LGCP model. And it’s one that may even be easier to get to be numerically stable that the closer, but more involved, approximations. So no, that is not likely to be the cause of prediction numerical problems.

Finn

>> On 11 Nov 2019, at 15:50, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Sec 8.4 aggregates the points into counts for a dual mesh, which turns the continuous Point process model into a discrete count model, via a zero-order integration approximation. The general LGCP likelihood approximation doesn’t do that.
>>
>> Finn
>>

>>> Best,
>>>
>>> James

On Thursday, November 7, 2019 at 3:35:27 PM UTC-8, Julianne Meisner wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I'm sure there's something I'm doing wrong but I can't figure it out. I'm fitting a separable space-time model in R-INLA, with the goal of doing prediction via sampling using inla.posterior.sample. The first issue has to do with the model fitting, which I am doing as follows:
>
> knots=min(cattle_data@data$time):max(cattle_data@data$time)
>
> mesh = inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain = loc.mesh,
>                     max.edge = c(0.3,0.6),
>                     offset = c(1, 1))
>
> spde_RE<-inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha=2)
>
> A<-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=coords_cattle, group=cattle_data@data$time, n.group=length(knots))
>
> iset <- inla.spde.make.index('i', n.spde=spde_RE$n.spde, n.group=length(knots))
>
> stk.dat.c<-inla.stack(
>   data=list(resp=cattle_data@data$n.cattle),
>   A=list(A,1),
>   effects=list(c(iset, list(intercept=1)), list(cattle_data@data)),
>   tag='est')
>
> pcprior<-list(theta = list(prior = "pc.prec", params = c(3, 0.05)))
>
> f.spde <- resp ~ 0 + intercept + urban + f(i, model=spde_RE, hyper = pcprior, group=i.group, control.group=list(model="ar1"))
>
> res<-inla (f.spde, data=inla.stack.data(stk.dat.c), family="zeroinflatedpoisson1", offset=log(cattle_data@data$mem.cattle), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.dat.c)),
>                       num.threads = inla.getOption("num.threads"), control.compute=list(config = TRUE), verbose=TRUE)
>
> -------------------------
> The dataset has 6,290 rows, the mesh has 1,428 vertices, and there are 17 knots in total. There is at least one row in the dataset (cattle_data) corresponding to each knot (i.e., each "time" value). My goal is to do prediction via sampling using inla.posterior.sample.
>
> The A matrix is 6290 x 24276 as expected, but res$summary.random$i has 1,428 rows (that is, equal to the number of mesh vertices). I believe this should have # rows = # mesh vertices * # knots, that is 24,276. Is that correct? Similarly, the corresponding entry in res$misc$configs$contents$length is 1,428.
>
> The second issue has to do with the mesh for prediction. My code for this is:
> Aprd<-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc.pred, group=kIdx, n.group=length(knots))
>
> Where "kIdx" is the group index (1-17), and there are 90,000 locations for prediction. This is a 1428 x 24276 matrix.
>
> My thought is if the corresponding draw from inla.posterior.sample is of length 24276, I can then do draw%*%Aprd for prediction. Is my Aprd code a matrix to project from the space-time mesh, to a space only mesh at the indicated knot, and then I need a second matrix to project to the prediction locations?
>
> Alternatively, if you can point me to an example of sampling via prediction on a separable space-time model, that would be helpful. As you may be able to tell, I am not a statistician!
>
> Thanks,
> Julianne
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How do I implement a uniform prior for spatial precision in INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Do not use a semi-colon after ‘expression’ but a colon. Also, you can check here for more details about using expression:

https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-priors.html#priors-defined-with-expression

This includes the implementation of a uniform (improper)  prior on the st. deviation. Remember that you need to compute the log-density of the prior and that the internal parameter must be unbounded.

Best,

Virgilio

> firstly I had to find the distribution for precision which is the inverse uniform distribution of sigma (since tau = 1/sigma) which is given as
> f(tau) = tau^(-2)*(b-a)^(-1).
> I then tried using the expression syntax to implement that in r-INLA as shown below, (which you can copy and paste into your R-console to verify what I am saying all things been equal)
>
> > > y = rnorm(1)
> > > a = 0.001
> > > b = 100
> > > uniprior = "expression;
> > > a = 0.001;
> > > b = 100
> > > sigma = 1;
> > > dens = sigma^-2*(1/(b-a));
> > > return(dens);"

> > > b=100
> > > sigma=1;
> > > dens=sigma^-2*(1/(b-a));
> > > #dens=1/(b-a);
> > > #logdens=log(dens);
> > > return(dens);' is unknown. Valid choices are: normal gaussian wishart1d wishart2d wishart3d wishart4d wishart5d loggamma minuslogsqrtruncnormal logtnormal logtgaussian flat logflat logiflat mvnorm pcar dirichlet none invalid betacorrelation logitbeta pcprec pcdof pccor0 pccor1 pcfgnh pcspdega pcmatern pcrange pcgamma pcmgamma pcgammacount pc refar pom jeffreystdf expression: table:.

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: How do I implement a uniform prior for spatial precision in INLA?
messages.body_plain:
note that the 'expression:' should return the log(prior(theta))  where
theta is the internal parameterisation.

if

	f(tau) = tau^-2

say, then with

	theta = log(tau)

you need to do a change of variable to get

	g(theta)

and then return

	log(g(theta))

note that the varible 'theta' in the expression, should NOT be
initialised, as its initialised by the value of the log(prior) to be
evaluated for.

see the doc for 'expression:' for an example.

if unsure, do an 'expression:' for a standard prior and check that you
get the same result.

H

messages.body_plain:
> Sec 8.4 aggregates the points into counts for a dual mesh, which turns the continuous Point process model into a discrete count model, via a zero-order integration approximation. The general LGCP likelihood approximation doesn’t do that.

This example in the book was motivated to face issues with large data.
At the time it was written we haven't yet the 'adaptive' strategy
available in INLA. Now, one can avoid the 'binding' approach of
aggregating data into dual mesh polygons for large point process data by
considering control.inla(strategy='adaptive'). Furthermore, the examples
on LGCP in the book and fancier ones can be easier done with the inlabru
package.

Elias

messages.subject: Bias in spatial covariance estimates in simulations
messages.subject_clean: Bias in spatial covariance estimates in simulations
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am simulating data with zero mean and Matern spatial covariance parameters such that:

alpha = 2 (so nu = 1)
nugget effect (sigma^2_epsilon) = .01
marginal variance (sigma^2_omega) = .5
spatial range parameter kappa = 1

I am using functions inla.mesh.2d, inla.spde2.matern, inla.spde.make.A and inla to estimate these spatial parameters. I have modeled them with multiple different settings: I have tried using different values for the mesh max.edges, cutoff, offset, using the loc vs loc.domain. I have tried different prior precisions for theta1 and theta2 as well. I have also tried centering and/or scaling the spatial coordinates (they were originally on 0 to 15 by 0 to 15 square, with approximately 10000 data points).

When I look at my results for 150 simulations for each of the multiple different mesh settings and prior settings, my results are typically biased in the following way:

the average nugget estimate is in the range 0.019-0.05 (truth .01)
the marginal variance is estimated around .6-.7 (truth .5)
the range is usually estimated around .75 (truth 1) [or estimated around 12 when the truth is 15 if I scale the coordinates]

Do you have any ideas as why these biases exist? I have tried so many combinations that I thought I would have found something that works by now. Thanks for any insight, please let me know if you have questions. Thanks very much for your help and expertise!

Steve

...and also, check the credible intervals rather than just the posterior mean, to see if the bias is small compared with the uncertainty ty. Also, the posterior mean should not be expected to be an unbiased estimator, so you need to consider your priors as well. The posterior mean is also dependent on the transformation scale. The posteriors for precision parameters tend to be more symmetric on the log scale, so you should do the comparison on that scale as well.
Finally, take a look at the author’s discussion response in the 2011 Lindgren et al paper, where we discussed biases due to coarse mesh resolution.

messages.subject: Spatio-temporal models for monthly temperatures, problems with AR1 model
messages.subject_clean: Spatio-temporal models for monthly temperatures, problems with AR1 model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working on a spatio-temporal model for the interpolation of monthly temperatures in Italy, using a dataset of 144 point stations/time series covering 58 years (1961-2018).

The model is very simple:

 temp~0+Intercept+sdem+sdis_costa+yy+f(i,model=spde, group=i.group,control.group=list(model="ar1")) #MODEL 1

with sdem (standardized station elevation), sdis_costa (standardized distance from the coast) and yy (year, ranging between 1961 and 2018).

The temporal index varies between 1 and 696 (58 years x 12 months).

The mesh was generated without the use of a shapefile (despite the Italian coast be visible in the attached image):

 as_Spatial(s.utm.ana)->sp.utm.ana

 inla.nonconvex.hull(points=sp.utm.ana)->italiaInla #no shapefile

 inla.mesh.2d(boundary = italiaInla,cutoff = 8000,max.edge = c(40000),offset =c(200000),min.angle =21)->mesh

As a first approach, I have not considered the presence of the sea between the Italian Peninsula and its islands.

Unfortunately using such a model, the latent field shows unreasonable values (values higher than 400!). The model fits very well the training dataset but, for the validation dataset, a limited set of stations shows very high RMSE values. Finally, the model exhibits a PIT values distribution far from the uniform.

After a lot of trials I identified this model (MODEL 2):

 list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.01)))->hyper.list
 temp~0+Intercept+sdem+sdis_costa+yy+f(mm,model="rw1",hyper=hyper.list)+f(i,model=spde, group=i.group,control.group=list(model="iid"))  #mm: month of the year: 1,2 ..12  #

With this model, the above-said problems disappear (almost uniform PIT values distribution, low RMSE values in the validation and training phases, reasonable latent field values). The interpolated temperature maps produced through this model are comparable with the maps produced through a simpler regression kriging approach (only spatial, using gstat package).

The problem seems to be connected with the AR1 model in the control.group, causing data overfitting.

As suggested in many posts, I tried a further approach (MODEL 3): PC priors for both the AR1 model and the spde

inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,prior.range=c(200000,0.2),prior.sigma=c(5,0.1),alpha=2)->spde              #CRS, epsg:32632/coordinates in meters

messages.body_plain:
I am struggling to find the best way to specify an autoregressive effect focused on members of a group relative to time.

Assume we have a number of subjects ("ID") who are measured repeatedly (the "Reading") over a period of several days ("Days").

Readings for each subject are expected to be correlated.  Readings for each subject on various days, including but possibly not limited to more recent days, are also expected to be correlated. Overall mean readings between recent days regardless of subject may also be correlated. There are no spatial effects.

Options include:

Random intercepts for all

inla(Reading ~ f(ID, model="iid") + f(Days, model="iid")

Random intercept for subject, random walk for time

inla(Reading ~ f(ID, model="iid") + f(Days, model="rw2")

Random intercept for subject, Ar1 for time

inla(Reading ~ f(ID, model="iid") + f(Days, model="ar1")

But how do we model the recency information specific to measurements of various IDs?
We could create a nested model with a separately-created interaction variable, which would capture at least some of this information, but would not distinguish days by recency:

Nested Model, one for each ID and Day

inla(Reading ~ f(ID, model="iid") + f(Days, model="ar1") + f(ID_Day, model="iid")

We could also make the interaction variable itself autoregressive, taking advantage of the fact that the ID_Day variable, if simply pasted from those two columns, will have some consecutive nature to it for each ID, albeit perhaps messy at the boundaries between IDs:

Nested Model, one for each ID and Day, AR1 effect

inla(Reading ~ f(ID, model="iid") + f(Days, model="ar1") + f(ID_Day, model="ar1")

>From what I can see, the nested model can help a fair amount, and the nested with the Ar1 effect on the interaction variable can help slightly more.  But neither seems to specify recency limited only to particular IDs, or to reflect the fact that particular IDs may have their own unique recency effect over time, in addition to whatever recency effect the average group member has.
I suspect there is a way to specify an (additional) AR1 effect solely on Days within individual IDs, but I am struggling to identify it.  Perhaps the replicate or copy commands are needed?

I have noticed ia "group" command within the "f" function, but I got an error when I tried to use it.  I'm not sure if that is because the IDs need to be consecutive or because this argument has nothing to do with what I am trying to accomplish.

I'd appreciate any insight. Thanks.

It looks like the answer indeed is to use replicate.  For the example below, create a replicate version of the ID variable with its own index and then use that to introduce the AR1 term.  So:

Idx.repl <- seq_along(unique(ID))

inla(Reading ~ f(ID, model=”iid”) + Days + f(ID.repl, model=”ar1”, replicate=Days)

Checked an analogous model in glmmTMBB and got comparable results with this:

glmmTMB(Reading ~ (1|ID) + Days + ar1( Days + 0 | batter))

Jonathan

messages.subject_clean: Validation of models with repeated Bernoulli trials
messages.body_plain:
Hello!  I am running some spatiotemporal models to investigate the presence/absence of an organism over time.  Each site was sampled multiple times per year, so my data is summarized as number of successes (observations of the organism) and number of total trials.  I read that inla binomial models can be coded with the number of successes as the dependent variable, and specifying the number of trials using the Ntrials argument.  Sample code is below.

formula <- n.successes ~ covariates

model <- inla(formula, Ntrials = data$n.sampling.events,
                                 control.inla = list(reordering = "metis"),
                                 family = "binomial",
                                 data = inla.stack.data(stck3),
                                 control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
                                 control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stck3), compute = TRUE))

I was wondering if anyone could assist me in learning how to validate this kind of model.  I know that inla has the cpo/pit function built in.  I tried this, got a bunch of failures, and tried recomputing the cpo values using inla.cpo() but it was taking way too long.  Are there any other methods that the community recommends?  Zuur et al. (2017) suggested simulating some data and comparing simulated and observed values, but did not provide an explanation on how to do so with this type of model.  I've also seen some papers doing k-fold cross validation with MAE and log-loss, but again, no description of how to conduct these analyses.  Thank you for your time.

messages.subject_clean: Time-varying adjacency matrix in spatio-temporal models?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

Let's consider 10 animals which body mass, status (whether they are healthy or not) and hair thickness is recorded over time. These animals are connected to each other by social interactions which also vary over time and which we used to build several adjacency matrices. The variables "hair thickness" and "body mass" are time series and between-individuals correlation is partially driven by social interactions and how they vary over time (time-varying adjacency matrices).

Going through several tutorials I have found a way to specify time-varying spatial points (based on X and Y coordinates) in SPDE models by grouping the points according to the time variable. However, I could not find a way to build an SPDE model relying on adjacency matrices so I thought of using Besag models instead.

Is there a way to specify BESAG models that my adjacency structure is varying over time with INLA? If yes, can anyone provide me with either a piece of code?

Thank you,
Camille

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In this case, I already know the graph at each time point. I would like to know if there is a way to take the structure of the social interactions into account when fitting a model to my data, for instance under the form of a random effect.

Let's say I want to know if the "health status" of an individual (ill or healthy) has an impact on its "hair thickness" and for some reason, I expect it to be affected by how individuals interact with each other around food patches. An animal well socialized has access to the patch more easily than more isolated animals, and alimentation has a direct impact on fur quality. Thus, individuals that interact a lot (i.e. high weights in the adjacency matrix / close to each other in the network) are more likely to show similar patterns. To some extend, I expect this correlation to be similar to correlations found in usual spatial analysis.

In addition, the fur thickness of an individual on time t is correlated to its thickness on time t-1. So there is a temporal autocorrelation at the individual level.

In my case, I have one measure of fur thickness per day per individual, one adjacency matrix per day and individual health status (binary, constant over time). Since the adjacency matrix is different every day, the structure of the "spatial" correlation is changing over time. For the sake of simplicity, I would consider adjacency matrices to be independent from each other (although it is not true).

The model should thus look like this:
thickness ~ 1 + health_status +
                   f(Individual_ID1, time, model = rw1) +
                   f(Individual_ID2, model = besag (?), graph = Array_of_adjacency_matrices (?), group = time etc.)

Is there any way to implement this using INLA? I have seen this kind of model with SPDE models but I cannot make an SPDE using my adjacency matrices (as far as I know).

Thank you,
C.

messages.subject: Necessary to keep seperable effects for time/space in non-seperable space-time models?
messages.subject_clean: Necessary to keep seperable effects for time/space in non-seperable space-time models?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone, I'm still new to INLA, and therefore I set my models up, on what I consider best practice from books etc. And adapt from there for my needs.

In Blangiardo and Cameletti's "Spatial and Spatio-temporal Bayesian Models with R" (2015) they explain non-separable space-time models with Knorr Held Type interactions of type I-IV (chapter 7.2.1, p. 240). For example:

formula.intIV<- y ~ f(ID.area,model="bym",graph=Georgia.adj) +
    f(ID.year,model="rw2") +
    f(ID.year1,model="iid") +
    f(ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int>,model="besag", graph=Georgia.adj, group=ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int>, control.group=list(model="rw2"))

They explain themselves that Knorr Held interactions of type II assumes an autoregressive structure on time. So I was wondering, what's the conceptual reason for keeping extra effects (random and auto-correlated) for time, in all of the example?

When I played around with such interactions (but with an SPDE, not with a "bym" model) I noticed that dropping those extra effect for time did not change the DIC or WAIC.

So my question is: should one in general still keep the separable time-effects, despite using a spatial-temporal effect? When would it (not) be advisable? How about the separable spatial term?

Best,
Vincent

> Hi,
>
> I am working on a spatio-temporal model for the interpolation of
> monthly temperatures in Italy, using a dataset of 144 point
> stations/time series covering 58 years (1961-2018).
>
> The model is very simple:
>
>  temp~0+Intercept+sdem+sdis_costa+yy+f(i,model=spde,
> group=i.group,control.group=list(model="ar1")) #MODEL 1
>
> with sdem (standardized station elevation), sdis_costa (standardized
> distance from the coast) and yy (year, ranging between 1961 and
> 2018).
>
> The temporal index varies between 1 and 696 (58 years x 12 months).
>
> The mesh was generated without the use of a shapefile (despite the
> Italian coast be visible in the attached image):
>
>  as_Spatial(s.utm.ana)->sp.utm.ana
>
>  inla.nonconvex.hull(points=sp.utm.ana)->italiaInla #no shapefile
>
>  inla.mesh.2d(boundary = italiaInla,cutoff = 8000,max.edge =
> c(40000),offset =c(200000),min.angle =21)->mesh
>
> As a first approach, I have not considered the presence of the sea
> between the Italian Peninsula and its islands.
>
> Unfortunately using such a model, the latent field shows
> unreasonable values (values higher than 400!). The model fits very
> well the training dataset but, for the validation dataset, a limited
> set of stations shows very high RMSE values. Finally, the model
> exhibits a PIT values distribution far from the uniform.
>
> After a lot of trials I identified this model (MODEL 2):
>
>  list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.01)))->hyper.list
>  temp~0+Intercept+sdem+sdis_costa+yy+f(mm,model="rw1",hyper=hyper.li <http://hyper.li>
> st)+f(i,model=spde, group=i.group,control.group=list(model="iid"))
> #mm: month of the year: 1,2 ..12  #
>
> With this model, the above-said problems disappear (almost uniform
> PIT values distribution, low RMSE values in the validation and
> training phases, reasonable latent field values). The interpolated
> temperature maps produced through this model are comparable with the
> maps produced through a simpler regression kriging approach (only
> spatial, using gstat package).
>
> The problem seems to be connected with the AR1 model in the
> control.group, causing data overfitting.
>
> As suggested in many posts, I tried a further approach (MODEL 3): PC
> priors for both the AR1 model and the spde
>
> inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,prior.range=c(200000,0.2),prior.sigma=c(5,0
> .1),alpha=2)->spde              #CRS, epsg:32632/coordinates in
> meters
>
> temp~0+Intercept+sdem+sdis_costa+yy+f(i,model=spde,
> group=i.group,control.group=list(model="ar1",hyper=list(theta=list(p
> rior='pc.cor1', param=c(0.7, 0.8)))))
>
> Actually, the use of PC priors improves the latent field, but its
> values are still too high than expected (SEE attached image). Some
> stations still show fitting problems in the validation phase (see
> the fitted vs observed values scatterplot) and the PIT distribution
> is not good (see image).
>
> I would appreciate a suggestion on what I am doing wrong. I have
> spent a lot of time doing several trials on the mesh resolution,
> priors for the fixed effects but I cannot solve the problem with the
> AR1 model.
>
>
> Thanks in advance
> Guido

"wrong" can be many different types of problems.

One is coding. This you can check by fixing the hyperparameter in the ar1 to give a rho close to 0. This should reproduce the iid group model.

One is whether your measures of fit are good. In the third figure, you do a spline regression wrt the x axis. What if you instead do a spline regression wrt the y=x axis? If you think of it this way, it seems the model has three types of points: good, biased up, and biased down.

A third type of "wrong" is whether the model is a good model for the data or not. This is very hard to know... no model is correct etc. In space-time models, I think it is common to find some mismatch between the model and the data. What if you reconsider the data as time-series with some spatial structure? Plot the time series and see if there are any patterns that jump out at you. Are there any time-series artifacts? E.g. are there any change in measurement conditions that result in jumps in the time series?

Best,
Haakon

Hi Guido,

Some further things to consider:
The effect of “distance to coast” is highly unlikely to be linear.
Measuring distances in metres when working on the scale of an entire country is virtually certain to lead to numerical floating point problems. I highly recommend converting UTM coordinates to kilometres.

Finn

Thanks for the reply!

I tried to modify the rank of 3-likelihood model in the example to rank 2: in inla.stack(), each data list has only 2 elements, and in the final inla() model,  use rep('gaussian', 2) instead of rep('gaussian', 3). The model will run without any error, but there's no random element output for the 3rd element (I guess INLA recognize the model as 2-variable and totally ignored the 3rd element that resembles the other.)

Is there something wrong with my modification? I wonder how to get all predictions from INLA with the low rank A matrix in LMC model.

The modified code with rank 2 model is here for your reference:
stack1 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = cbind(as.vector(y1), NA)),
  A = list(A1),
  effects = list(list(intercept1 = 1, s1 = 1:spde$n.spde)))

stack2 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = cbind(NA, as.vector(y2))),
  A = list(A2),
  effects = list(list(intercept2 = 1, s2 = 1:spde$n.spde,
    s12 = 1:spde$n.spde)))

stack3 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = cbind(NA, as.vector(y3))),
  A = list(A3),
  effects = list(list(intercept3 = 1, s3 = 1:spde$n.spde,
    s23 = 1:spde$n.spde)))
stack <- inla.stack(stack1, stack2, stack3)
result <- inla(form, rep('gaussian', 2), # use to be 3
  data = inla.stack.data(stack),
  control.family = list(hyper.eps, hyper.eps),
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack)),
  control.mode = list(theta = theta.ini, restart = TRUE),
  control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb'))

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot for your attention and suggestions.

Actually, I see two kind of problems:
1) the model with iid on control.group is the model which gives very good results for the validation and the training dataset. The model returns parameters estimates which are sensible and the interpolated maps make sense. The problem of this model is that the a non negligeable amount of stations show correlated residuals, more precisely, a Residual seasonal behavior. This depends on the fact that the rw1 smoother tends to fit the montainous series, underestimating the cycle of the south of Italy. This underestimation results in Residual cyclical behavior for some stations. However, if I consider the model residuals all together, I would say that model hypothesis of iid residuals are satisfied. Am I paying too much attention to the details, considering the residuals of each single series?

2) the problem related to the model with ar1 or rw1 on control.group is the opposite. The residuals are uncorrelated for most of the data series, the model has good performance on the training dataset but the latent field has non reliable values. This fact produces bad results (high residuals) for some stations, which is not good for prediction purposes.

I was wonderin whether distinguishing between north and south time series (two different smoothers using replicate) could be a reasonable tentative.

Thanks
Guido

On Mon, 2019-11-25 at 19:53 -0800, Cyril Marsh wrote:
> prediction = exp(Beta0 + Pu)
>
> Can I get marginal distribution for sum(prediction)?

essentially, only by simulation. you can use

inla.posterior.sample

and then

inla.posterior.sample.eval

to evaluate \sum exp(\linearPredictor_i)

you may need to weight the sum taking into account the areas of the mesh, etc.

see the 'LGCP' paper by Dan Simpson et al, in Biometrika a few years ago

H

messages.subject: High transect predictions when including covariates INLABRU
messages.subject_clean: High transect predictions when including covariates INLABRU
messages.body_plain:
Apologies for the long email, I have tried to include all the potentially relevant details of this issue.

We have multiple seasons of survey data. We do not want to include a temporal effect between seasons. We wish to treat each season as an independent replicate.

We would like to build a LGCP model to generate spatial predictions, and assess the effect of a number of environmental covariates.

We wish to use an SPDE to account for spatial autocorrelations not accounted for by environmental covariates. The ideal scenario would so that the output of an SPDE only model, and a model with multiple covariates would be similar, and we could assess the independent contributions of spatial covariates.

Our transects are 0.9km wide with a 5km spacing. We do not have distance data for the samples.

Firstly we built a LGCP model as follows:

max.edge <- max(round(diff(range(point.data @coords[,1]))/20), round(diff(range(rbind(point.data @coords[,2]))/20)))

## max.edge = 15

bound.outer = max(round(diff(range(point.data @coords[,1]))), round(diff(range(point.data @coords[,2]))))

## bound.outer = 250

my.boundary <- gBuffer(my.transects, width = 10, byid = F)

mesh = inla.mesh.2d(max.edge = c(1,5)*max.edge,

                     boundary = my.boundary,

                     cutoff = 1,

                     offset = c(max.edge * 5, bound.outer),

                     crs = inla.CRS(projargs = CRS(proj4string(point.data))))

pcmatern <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,

                                    alpha = 2,

                                    prior.sigma = c(0.01, 0.01),

                                    prior.range = c(20, 0.05))

Season <- point.data$Season

nseas <- length(unique(point.data$Season))

mdl.components <- ~ spat(map = coordinates, group = Season, ngroup = nseas, model = pcmatern, control.group = list(model = "iid"))

my.transects$weight <- 0.9

ips <- ipoints(my.transects, mesh, group = "Season")

fit.model.spde <- inlabru::lgcp(components = mdl.components,

                                 data = point.data,

                                 ips = ips,

                                 formula = mdl.formula,

                                 options = list(control.compute = list(dic = TRUE,

                                                                       waic = TRUE,

                                                                       config = TRUE)))

This model seems to work ok. When using the model to predict the intensity for integration points along our transects for each season, the total predictions for each season are similar to what we have observed. The total estimate of points across the entire survey area is also similar to what we would expect.

ips.t.1 = subset(ips,ips$Season == 1)

ips.t.2 = subset(ips,ips$Season == 2)

ips.t.3 = subset(ips,ips$Season == 3)

total.1 = predict(fit.model.spde, ips.t.1, ~ sum(weight * exp(spat + Intercept)))

We then added 5 spatial covariates. Each covariate was modelled as a linear response.

These values were extracted for both the integration points “ips”, and the point data “point.data” before running the lgcp model and stored within the dataframe attached to “point.data”. Each point’s covariate value was centred by the mean value across the entire mesh extent. The values were returned during lgcp() and predict() by defining a series of functions.

We then compared 6 separate models by dropping one covariate at a time. The most complex models generally had lower WAIC and DIC scores. The coeffients of each spatial covariate did not overlap with zero in any case.

The problem is that when covariates are included, the intensity predictions at integration points along our transects are far higher than what we would expect. The predictions across the entire survey region are also far higher.

I am suspicious that the reason for this result could be due to the construction of the pcmatern?

Or perhaps I have misspecified something within the code?

Our transects preferentially sample more suitable areas so this may also present issues when we interpret our covariates

Any guidance here would be appreciated.

Many thanks

Feng

messages.subject: Multiple AR frailties by group
messages.subject_clean: Multiple AR frailties by group
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a data set containing purchasing events by multiple subjects.  I'm modelling these purchases as repeated events by fitting a Weibull frailty model to the data.
I've implemented autoregressive dependence on the residuals (AR(1) frailty) resulting in one AR coefficient (rho) for all subjects. However,  I've assigned the individuals to different groups based on purchasing behavior.
I was wondering if INLA is able to incorporate different autoregressive dependencies by subject group, thus assuming group-specific AR(1)'s?

Kind regards,

David

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Multiple AR frailties by group
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Multiple AR frailties by group
messages.body_plain:
good question.

using time-dependent frailty will usually require a prior for the
correlation parameter that contracts to 1, see inla.doc("pc.cor1")

using 'replicate', like

	f(time, model="ar1", replicate=subject)

with subject = 1, 2,...

then each person have its own realiation of the ar1 model, but they
all share the same hyperparameters (precision, correlation)

if you want to split this, then you need several terms,

	f(time1, model="ar1", replicate=subject1) +
	f(time2,
model="ar1", replicate=subject2)

where time1=time, time2=time, f.ex,

and subject1 = 1,2..., are those in 'group1'
and subject2 = 1, 2,... are those in 'group2'

then the (prec, corr) parameters will be separate for each group, but
the same within each group.

so, you cannot have to many groups then...

H
